claim: Transposable elements (TEs) can become transcriptionally active as an animal ages.
source: Transposable elements (TEs) are mobile sequences of DNA that can become transcriptionally active as an animal ages.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known phenomenon.

claim: Increased TE activity shortens the life span of male Drosophila melanogaster.
source: We find that increased TE activity shortens the life span of male Drosophila melanogaster.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: The effect of increased TE activity on mortality is only apparent in middle-aged animals.
source: The effect is only apparent in middle-aged animals. The increase in mortality is not seen in young animals.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by age-specific mortality data in Figure 4b-e.

claim: An intact reverse transcriptase is necessary for the decrease in life span caused by TE activity.
source: An intact reverse transcriptase is necessary for the decrease in life span, implicating a DNA-mediated process in the effect.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 6.

claim: TE activity increases sensitivity to oxidative stress.
source: TE activity increases sensitivity to oxidative stress and promotes a decline in circadian rhythmicity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by paraquat resistance assays in Figure 7a.

claim: TE activity promotes a decline in circadian rhythmicity.
source: TE activity increases sensitivity to oxidative stress and promotes a decline in circadian rhythmicity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by circadian behavior data in Figure 7b-c.

claim: Overexpression of dFOXO can partially rescue the detrimental effects of increased TE activity on life span.
source: The overexpression of the Forkhead-box O family (FOXO) stress response transcription factor can partially rescue the detrimental effects of increased TE activity on life span.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 8b.

claim: TE mRNA levels increase in the aging somatic tissue of flies.
source: Multiple studies (Gorbunova et al., 2021) report that TE mRNA levels increase in the aging somatic tissue of flies (Giordani et al., 2021; Li et al., 2013; Wood et al., 2016), termites (Elsner et al., 2018), mice (De Cecco et al., 2013b), rats (Mumford et al., 2019), and humans (LaRocca et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: TE mRNA levels increase in the aging somatic tissue of termites.
source: Multiple studies (Gorbunova et al., 2021) report that TE mRNA levels increase in the aging somatic tissue of flies (Giordani et al., 2021; Li et al., 2013; Wood et al., 2016), termites (Elsner et al., 2018), mice (De Cecco et al., 2013b), rats (Mumford et al., 2019), and humans (LaRocca et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Elsner et al., 2018.

claim: TE mRNA levels increase in the aging somatic tissue of mice.
source: Multiple studies (Gorbunova et al., 2021) report that TE mRNA levels increase in the aging somatic tissue of flies (Giordani et al., 2021; Li et al., 2013; Wood et al., 2016), termites (Elsner et al., 2018), mice (De Cecco et al., 2013b), rats (Mumford et al., 2019), and humans (LaRocca et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to De Cecco et al., 2013b.

claim: TE mRNA levels increase in the aging somatic tissue of rats.
source: Multiple studies (Gorbunova et al., 2021) report that TE mRNA levels increase in the aging somatic tissue of flies (Giordani et al., 2021; Li et al., 2013; Wood et al., 2016), termites (Elsner et al., 2018), mice (De Cecco et al., 2013b), rats (Mumford et al., 2019), and humans (LaRocca et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mumford et al., 2019.

claim: TE mRNA levels increase in the aging somatic tissue of humans.
source: Multiple studies (Gorbunova et al., 2021) report that TE mRNA levels increase in the aging somatic tissue of flies (Giordani et al., 2021; Li et al., 2013; Wood et al., 2016), termites (Elsner et al., 2018), mice (De Cecco et al., 2013b), rats (Mumford et al., 2019), and humans (LaRocca et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to LaRocca et al., 2020.

claim: Gypsy insertions increase during aging in the Drosophila melanogaster brain and fat body.
source: Two reporter systems for insertions of the long-terminal-repeat (LTR) retrotransposon gypsy demonstrate that gypsy insertions increase during aging in the Drosophila melanogaster brain and fat body (Chang et al., 2019a; Li et al., 2013; Wood et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chang et al., 2019a; Li et al., 2013; Wood et al., 2016.

claim: TE movement in somatic tissue has been proposed to be a driver of genomic instability through DNA damage.
source: TE movement in somatic tissue has been proposed to be a driver of genomic instability through DNA damage (Ivics and Izsvák, 2010) and potentially aging (Morley, 1995; Wood and Helfand, 2013; Woodruff and Nikitin, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ivics and Izsvák, 2010; Morley, 1995; Wood and Helfand, 2013; Woodruff and Nikitin, 1995.

claim: TE activity has been reported to cause disease in humans.
source: Additionally, TE activity has been reported to cause disease in humans (Hancks and Kazazian, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hancks and Kazazian, 2012.

claim: L1 activity can trigger an inflammation response that contributes to aging-related phenotypes in human senescent cells.
source: Current research reports that long-interspersed-element-1 (L1) activity itself, without an increase in insertions, can trigger an inflammation response that contributes to aging-related phenotypes in human senescent cells (De Cecco et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to De Cecco et al., 2019.

claim: The use of reverse transcriptase inhibitors can downregulate age-associated inflammation in aged mice.
source: In aged mice, the use of reverse transcriptase inhibitors can downregulate this age-associated inflammation (De Cecco et al., 2019) implicating retrotransposons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to De Cecco et al., 2019.

claim: The shortened life span of a Dicer-2 mutant fly strain can be extended by the use of reverse transcriptase inhibitors.
source: The shortened life span of a Dicer-2 (dcr-2) mutant fly strain, which has an increase in TE expression, can also be extended by the use of reverse transcriptase inhibitors (Wood et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wood et al., 2016.

claim: Heterochromatin-repressive marks decrease as an animal ages.
source: As an animal ages, heterochromatin-repressive marks decrease and resident silent genes can become expressed (Jiang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2013.

claim: TE sequences are enriched in silent heterochromatin and become expressed as heterochromatin breaks down.
source: TE sequences are enriched in silent heterochromatin and thus become expressed (De Cecco et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to De Cecco et al., 2013a.

claim: The PIWI pathway dominates in the germline for TE silencing.
source: The PIWI pathway dominates in the germline while the somatic tissue of Drosophila is thought to mainly rely on the siRNA pathway (Hyun, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hyun, 2017.

claim: The somatic tissue of Drosophila mainly relies on the siRNA pathway for TE silencing.
source: The PIWI pathway dominates in the germline while the somatic tissue of Drosophila is thought to mainly rely on the siRNA pathway (Hyun, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hyun, 2017.

claim: Endogenous siRNAs in RISC mapping to TE loci have been reported in D. melanogaster.
source: In D. melanogaster, endogenous siRNAs in RISC mapping to TE loci have been reported (Czech et al., 2008; Ghildiyal et al., 2008; Kawamura et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Czech et al., 2008; Ghildiyal et al., 2008; Kawamura et al., 2008.

claim: Mutation, knockdown, or depletion of Dcr-2 leads to increased expression of TE in somatic cells and a shortened life span.
source: The mutation, knockdown, or depletion of genes involved in the siRNA pathway such as Dcr-2 (Lee et al., 2004) and AGO2 (Okamura et al., 2004) leads to increased expression of TE in somatic cells and a shortened life span (Kawamura et al., 2008; Czech et al., 2008; Chung et al., 2008; Lim et al., 2011; Li et al., 2013; Wood et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutation, knockdown, or depletion of AGO2 leads to increased expression of TE in somatic cells and a shortened life span.
source: The mutation, knockdown, or depletion of genes involved in the siRNA pathway such as Dcr-2 (Lee et al., 2004) and AGO2 (Okamura et al., 2004) leads to increased expression of TE in somatic cells and a shortened life span (Kawamura et al., 2008; Czech et al., 2008; Chung et al., 2008; Lim et al., 2011; Li et al., 2013; Wood et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Overexpression of Dcr-2 in adult fly somatic tissue can lower TE expression and extend life span.
source: On the other hand, the overexpression of Dcr-2 (Wood et al., 2016) and AGO2 (Yang et al., 2022) in adult fly somatic tissue can lower TE expression and extend life span.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wood et al., 2016.

claim: Overexpression of AGO2 in adult fly somatic tissue can lower TE expression and extend life span.
source: On the other hand, the overexpression of Dcr-2 (Wood et al., 2016) and AGO2 (Yang et al., 2022) in adult fly somatic tissue can lower TE expression and extend life span.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yang et al., 2022.

claim: FOXO is an evolutionarily conserved transcription factor capable of enhancing longevity.
source: The Forkhead-box O family (FOXO) is an evolutionarily conserved transcription factor capable of enhancing longevity by enabling the cell to respond to diverse stress signals (Calnan and Brunet, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Calnan and Brunet, 2008.

claim: The longevity effects of FOXO have been reported in worms, flies, and mice.
source: The longevity effects of FOXO have been reported in worms, flies, and mice (Martins et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martins et al., 2016.

claim: dFOXO is an upstream activator of the small RNA pathways that limit TE expression in somatic tissues.
source: Importantly, dFOXO is an upstream activator of the small RNA pathways that limit TE expression in somatic tissues (Spellberg and Marr, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spellberg and Marr, 2015.

claim: In wDAH wildtype animals, only two TEs (1731 and Doc4 retrotransposons) show significantly increased expression with age.
source: In these conditions, the wt animals display significantly increased expression of only two TEs (the 1731 and Doc4 retrotransposons).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1a-b.

claim: In wDAH wildtype animals, two TEs (Stalker2 and G6 retrotransposons) show decreased expression with age.
source: At the same time, there is decreased expression of two TEs (the Stalker2 and G6 retrotransposons) with age (Figure 1a and b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1a-b.

claim: In dFOXO deletion animals, 18 TEs exhibited a significant increase in expression with age.
source: By contrast, in the dFOXO deletion animals, 18 TEs (the retrotransposons: Accord, Circ, Gate, Copia, Gypsy, MGD1, RooA, 1731, Burdock, TartC, Invader2, Invader4, Juan, G6, IVK, Doc3; and the DNA transposons: TransIB3, 1360) exhibited a significant increase in expression with age (Figure 1c and d, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) while no TE expression decreased with age.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1c-d.

claim: No TE expression decreased with age in dFOXO deletion animals.
source: By contrast, in the dFOXO deletion animals, 18 TEs (the retrotransposons: Accord, Circ, Gate, Copia, Gypsy, MGD1, RooA, 1731, Burdock, TartC, Invader2, Invader4, Juan, G6, IVK, Doc3; and the DNA transposons: TransIB3, 1360) exhibited a significant increase in expression with age (Figure 1c and d, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) while no TE expression decreased with age.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1c-d.

claim: The overall TE load is greater in aged dFOXO deletion flies.
source: This indicates that the overall TE load is greater in the aged dFOXO deletion flies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing more TEs increase with age in dFOXO deletion flies.

claim: Total TE expression increased 1.2-fold with age in wildtype flies.
source: Expression increased only 1.2-fold with age (Supplementary file 1) in wt flies and 1.41-fold in dFOXO null flies (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Total TE expression increased 1.41-fold with age in dFOXO null flies.
source: Expression increased only 1.2-fold with age (Supplementary file 1) in wt flies and 1.41-fold in dFOXO null flies (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: Ectopic gypsy expression is significantly induced when the UAS-gypsy line is crossed to a strain with ubiquitously expressed GAL4.
source: Using this approach, we found that ectopic gypsy expression is significantly induced when the line is crossed to a strain in which GAL4 is ubiquitously expressed under the ubiquitin promoter (Ubi>gypsy) (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: New insertions of ectopic gypsy are created and can be specifically detected in Ubi>gypsy flies.
source: Using this approach, we found that new insertions are created and can be specifically detected (Figure 2c) when UAS-gypsy is expressed (Ubi>gypsy genotype).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The UAS-gypsy element can transpose and is an active TE element.
source: Sanger sequencing of the qPCR insertion products demonstrates the specific detection of this junction, indicating that the UAS-gypsy element can transpose and is an active TE element (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2d.

claim: More than 11,000 insertion sites of UAS-gypsy were identified through targeted sequencing.
source: More than 11,000 insertion sites were identified.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the sequencing results.

claim: Insertion sites of UAS-gypsy were identified in all chromosomes.
source: Sites were identified in all chromosomes with the fraction of insertions roughly correlating with the size of the chromosome (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: 66% of the mapped insertion sites are in transcribed regions.
source: Also, 66% of the mapped insertion sites are in transcribed regions (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The majority of insertion sites in transcribed regions are in intronic regions.
source: Of those sites, the majority are in intronic regions (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The target site duplication consensus determined from mapped insertion sites matches the known YRYRYR previously identified for gypsy integration sites.
source: The target site duplication consensus determined from our mapped insertion sites matches the known YRYRYR previously identified for gypsy integration sites (Figure 3d; Dej et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section, shown in Figure 3d, and supported by citation to Dej et al., 1998.

claim: The somatic expression of an active gypsy significantly decreased the life span of male flies.
source: We consistently found that the somatic expression of an active gypsy significantly decreased the life span of male flies (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: A 19% reduction of life span in the active gypsy male flies is observed compared to parental controls.
source: A 19% reduction of life span in the active gypsy male flies is observed compared to parental controls, with a median survival of 70 days and 86 days, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the life span data.

claim: The life span effect of active gypsy only becomes apparent once the flies start to age.
source: The life span effect on the Ubi>gypsy flies only becomes apparent once the flies start to age. At 26 days old, the survival curves noticeably separate from the parental controls and calculation of the age-specific mortality shows a significant increase in mortality present in 26–75-day-old animals (Figure 4b–e).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4b-e.

claim: Ectopic gypsy DNA was detected at different ages in the survival curve (5, 14, 30, 50, and 70 days old).
source: Ectopic gypsy DNA was detected at different ages in the survival curve (5, 14, 30, 50, and 70 days old) with three different primer pairs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the molecular assays.

claim: Ectopic gypsy RNA expression remains constant throughout the assayed time points.
source: Interestingly, ectopic gypsy RNA expression remains constant throughout the assayed time points (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The deletion of RT in the UAS-gypsy transgene prevents the life span effect observed when crossed to Ubi-GAL4.
source: The deletion of RT in the UAS-gypsy transgene prevents the life span effect observed when crossed to Ubi-GAL4 (Ubi>ΔRT genotype) (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Ubi>ΔRT and Ubi>gypsy express the transposon RNA at the same level.
source: This is not due to a defect in mRNA levels because RT-qPCR indicates that Ubi>ΔRT and Ubi>gypsy express the transposon RNA at the same level (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6b.

claim: No increase in ectopic gypsy 3′ DNA is detected in the Ubi>ΔRT line despite expressing equivalent levels of mRNA as Ubi>gypsy.
source: Consistent with the loss of RT activity, we detect no increase in ectopic gypsy 3′ DNA in the Ubi>ΔRT line despite expressing equivalent levels of mRNA as Ubi>gypsy (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6c.

claim: An active RT is required for the observed decrease in life span seen when gypsy is ectopically expressed in somatic tissue.
source: This result indicates that an active RT is required for the observed decrease in life span seen when gypsy is ectopically expressed in somatic tissue.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RT deletion experiment results.

claim: Resistance to paraquat exposure decreased with age in all genotypes.
source: As expected, resistance to paraquat exposure decreased with age in all genotypes (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The survival curve of 5-day-old active gypsy flies mimicked that of 15-day-old parental control curves in paraquat resistance assays.
source: Interestingly, the survival curve of the 5-day-old active gypsy flies mimicked that of the 15-day-old parental control curves.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the paraquat resistance data.

claim: 15-day-old active gypsy flies had a significant decrease in resistance to paraquat exposure when compared to age-matched parental controls.
source: Meanwhile, the 15-day-old active gypsy flies had a significant decrease in resistance to paraquat exposure when compared to age-matched parental controls.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the paraquat resistance data.

claim: 84–97% of the control flies were rhythmic at all the assessed ages.
source: Also, 84–97% of the control flies were rhythmic at all the assessed ages, whereas only 73–77% of the flies with ectopic expression of the TE remain rhythmic (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Only 73–77% of the flies with ectopic expression of the TE remain rhythmic.
source: Also, 84–97% of the control flies were rhythmic at all the assessed ages, whereas only 73–77% of the flies with ectopic expression of the TE remain rhythmic (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Flies with ectopic gypsy expression display a significant decline in their rhythmicity index throughout the assessed ages.
source: Indeed, these flies also display a significant decline in their rhythmicity index (RI) throughout the assessed ages that does not happen in the control flies (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Increased expression of dFOXO can rescue the effect on life span due to gypsy activity.
source: We find that increased expression of dFOXO can rescue the effect on life span due to gypsy activity. The 19% decrease in life span reported in Figure 4a is reduced to 8% when compared to the UAS control and the life span matches the GAL4 control (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8b.

claim: The rescue effect of dFOXO is not due to a decrease in ectopic gypsy mRNA expression.
source: Importantly, the effect is not simply due to a decrease in ectopic gypsy mRNA expression as the transcript remains significantly induced in the dFOXO-overexpressing flies (compare Figure 2b with Figure 8c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figures 2b and 8c.

claim: dFOXO overexpression rescues the paraquat sensitivity in animals with active gypsy.
source: We find that dFOXO overexpression rescues the paraquat sensitivity in the animals with active gypsy.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the paraquat assay with dFOXO overexpression.

claim: Animals overexpressing dFOXO have a lower number of gypsy insertions despite expressing comparable levels of UAS-gypsy mRNA.
source: Surprisingly, despite the fact that the UAS-gypsy mRNA is expressed at comparable levels (compare Figure 8c and Figure 2b), animals overexpressing dFOXO have a lower number of insertions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figures 8c and 2b.

claim: Overexpression of dFOXO is both protecting genome integrity and fending off the oxidative stress caused by the active gypsy TE.
source: Overexpression of dFOXO is both protecting genome integrity and fending of the oxidative stress caused by the active gypsy TE.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data showing reduced insertions and rescued paraquat sensitivity.

claim: The wDAH and dFOXO deletion lines have been extensively backcrossed, making them isogenic other than for the dFOXO deletion.
source: These lines have been extensively backcrossed, making them isogenic other than for the dFOXO deletion (Slack et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Slack et al., 2011.

claim: The vast majority of TE expression levels in both strains fall within the observed range of average gene expression.
source: The vast majority of TE expression levels in both strains fall within the observed range of average gene expression (Figure 1a and d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1a and d.

claim: The otherwise isogenic lines have a different transcriptionally active TE landscape.
source: This means that the otherwise isogenic lines have a different transcriptionally active TE landscape.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of TE expression in young wt and dFOXO null flies.

claim: The gypsy retrotransposon has been clearly shown to become active in aged D. melanogaster somatic tissue under natural conditions.
source: The retrotransposon gypsy is a TE that has been clearly shown to become active in aged D. melanogaster somatic tissue under natural conditions (Li et al., 2013; Wood et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Li et al., 2013; Wood et al., 2016.

claim: The fraction of insertions roughly correlates with the size of the chromosome.
source: Sites were identified in all chromosomes with the fraction of insertions roughly correlating with the size of the chromosome (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Insertions are detected roughly evenly across the chromosomes at the 1 megabase resolution level.
source: At this level of resolution, insertions are detected roughly evenly across the chromosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the distribution of insertion sites.

claim: A life span effect was observed in females with the UAS-gypsy system.
source: A life span effect was also observed in females; surprisingly it was also present in the UAS-gypsy parental control (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: More detected insertions are present in female UAS-gypsy controls than their male equivalents.
source: Interestingly, a molecular assay demonstrates that more detected insertions are present in female UAS-gypsy controls than their male equivalents (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: No significant difference in detected insertions was found between head and body in male Ubi>gypsy flies.
source: No significant difference was detected in male flies, indicating an equivalent level of insertions throughout somatic tissue.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the distribution assay.

claim: In females, a significant bias toward insertions in the body was detected in Ubi>gypsy flies.
source: In females, however, a significant bias toward insertions in the body was detected, indicating possible differential expression of UAS-gypsy in the mixed tissues.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the distribution assay.

claim: The shape of the survival curve for the active gypsy flies indicated that the flies were healthy.
source: The shape of the survival curve for the active gypsy flies indicated that the flies were healthy and thus the increase in mortality was not due to disease or external factors.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section analyzing the survival data.

claim: 5-day-old animals with an active gypsy have the oxidative stress resistance of a 15-day-old animal.
source: Perhaps most dramatically, 5-day-old animals with an active gypsy have the oxidative stress resistance of a 15-day-old animal.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the paraquat resistance results.

claim: The decay of locomotor activity occurred at a rate similar to controls in active gypsy flies.
source: The decay of locomotor activity also occurred at a rate similar to controls, indicating that not all aging phenotypes show an accelerated decay in response to an active TE.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the negative geotaxis results.

claim: An active TE can accelerate a subset of aging phenotypes.
source: We find that an active TE can accelerate a subset of aging phenotypes and provide evidence that TEs are not merely bystanders in the aging process and can behave as causative agents once they are active.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental results.

claim: TEs are not merely bystanders in the aging process and can behave as causative agents once they are active.
source: We find that an active TE can accelerate a subset of aging phenotypes and provide evidence that TEs are not merely bystanders in the aging process and can behave as causative agents once they are active.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on the experimental results.

claim: The 19% decrease in life span is reduced to 8% when dFOXO is overexpressed.
source: The 19% decrease in life span reported in Figure 4a is reduced to 8% when compared to the UAS control and the life span matches the GAL4 control (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8b.

claim: FOXO responds to paraquat-induced oxidative stress.
source: This is perhaps not surprising because we and others have previously shown that FOXO responds to paraquat-induced oxidative stress (Chang et al., 2019b; Donovan and Marr, 2016; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Chang et al., 2019b; Donovan and Marr, 2016; Wang et al., 2005.

claim: The FOXO family of transcription factors regulate many pathways that could be reducing the detrimental effects of increased TE expression.
source: The FOXO family of transcription factors regulate many pathways that could be reducing the detrimental effects of increased TE expression such as the DNA damage response pathway, antioxidant pathways, and proteostasis pathways (Gui and Burgering, 2021; Webb et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Gui and Burgering, 2021; Webb et al., 2016.

claim: dFOXO activates pathways that are established antagonists to the detrimental effects of TEs such as the RNAi pathway.
source: In addition, dFOXO activates pathways that are established antagonists to the detrimental effects of TEs such as the RNAi pathway (Spellberg and Marr, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Spellberg and Marr, 2015.

claim: The induction of TE activity in somatic tissue resulted in a reduction in D. melanogaster life span when compared to parental controls.
source: The induction of TE activity in somatic tissue resulted in a reduction in D. melanogaster life span when compared to parental controls and a significant increase in mortality in middle-aged animals.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the life span results.

claim: There was a 19% decrease in the life span of male animals with active gypsy.
source: There was a 19% decrease in the life span of male animals.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the life span results.

claim: The mortality effects of the active TE are only evident in relatively aged animals despite the fact that the retrotransposon is active during early life.
source: Interestingly, the mortality effects of the active TE are only evident in relatively aged animals despite the fact that the retrotransposon is active during early life.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section analyzing the age-specific effects.

claim: Young animals can tolerate expression and insertion of the TE.
source: This suggests that the young animals can tolerate expression and insertion of the TE.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Discussion section based on the age-specific mortality data.

claim: It is only when the animals begin to age that TE expression becomes a burden and takes a toll.
source: It is only when the animals begin to age that TE expression becomes a burden and takes a toll.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Discussion section based on the age-specific mortality data.

claim: The combination of other metabolic and physiological effects of aging with TE activity may be detrimental.
source: Perhaps it is the combination of the other metabolic and physiological effects of aging with the TE activity that is detrimental.
evidence: This is speculation stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Detectable insertions do not seem to increase with age despite constant expression of the transgene.
source: Unexpectedly, detectable insertions do not seem to increase with age, despite constant (although much more variable) expression of the transgene as the animals age.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the insertion quantification results.

claim: The oldest animals have the lowest detectable insertions.
source: In fact, the oldest animals have the lowest detectable insertions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the insertion quantification results.

claim: Unknown mechanisms are acting to clear or at least prevent an increase in TE insertion load.
source: This suggests that unknown mechanisms are acting to clear or at least prevent an increase in TE insertion load.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Discussion section based on the insertion data.

claim: A functional RT is needed for the TE effect on life span.
source: By using a UAS-gypsy strain with a defective RT, we were able to determine that a functional RT is needed for the TE effect on life span.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the RT deletion results.

claim: The need for a functional RT to decrease life span implicates the DNA synthesis step as being detrimental.
source: The need for a functional RT to decrease life span implicates the DNA synthesis step as being detrimental.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Discussion section based on the RT deletion results.

claim: The reverse transcriptase inhibitor 3TC extends the life span of a Dcr-2 null fly strain.
source: The reverse transcriptase inhibitor 3TC extends the life span of a Dcr-2 null fly strain, which has an increase in TE expression (Wood et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Wood et al., 2016.

evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the dFOXO rescue results.

source: We also measured the relative integration number of 5-day-old animals expressing UAS-gypsy and overexpressing dFOXO. Surprisingly, despite the fact that the UAS-gypsy mRNA is expressed at comparable levels (compare Figure 8c and Figure 2b), animals overexpressing dFOXO have a lower number of insertions.
